title: Align Value, Profit, and People Propositions
coreMove: Check whether the buyer promise, profit model, and people system reinforce each other before calling a strategy sustainable.
sourcePressure: Sustain a blue ocean by aligning the value proposition for buyers, profit proposition for the organization, and people proposition for those who must deliver or support it.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Mistaking a loved customer offer for a complete strategy when costs or people incentives cannot support it.

sourceAnchors.name: value, profit, and people propositions
sourceAnchors.detail: official strategic-alignment support defines the three propositions and says sustainable strategy requires alignment across all three
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Buyer love is only one leg; the value, profit, and people propositions have to hold the same weight.

sourceAnchors.name: Tata Nano
sourceAnchors.detail: official support is safe for the point that value and profit propositions can face execution setbacks when the people proposition is weak
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Tata Nano is a useful warning: a striking buyer and profit idea can still stumble when the people side cannot carry the promise cleanly.

hook: Do not open with a competitor scoreboard, a war metaphor, or a generic market map.
Do not use A crowded market is not..., The real strategy is..., or What if growth... as reusable shells.
counterintuition: Avoid Most people assume... but actually... and The opposite is true.
Avoid turning every chapter into competition bad, creativity good.
tryThisNow: Avoid Set a timer for 60 seconds and list... as a repeated action.
Avoid generic reflect on your strategy prompts.
examples: Avoid conference-room whiteboard workshops as the default scene.
Avoid repeating mugs, markers, dosing cups, bike helmets, radiators, bus depots, classrooms, narrow kitchens, or generic dashboard scenes.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human

exampleSpecs.domain: grain-bowl lunch counter with buyer demand but kitchen strain
exampleSpecs.audience: a food operator whose popular offer strains the kitchen
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a successful menu survives the system behind it
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she sees that buyer value alone is not enough when margin and cooks break behind the counter
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Quinoa spills under the prep rail while the lunch line curls past the door

exampleSpecs.domain: mobile clinic evening visits and route economics
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic leader excited by demand for evening visits
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the service scales without losing money or burning out nurses
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he chooses route clustering and documentation redesign before expanding the valued offer
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 8:20 p.m., Mathieu watches the last nurse finish notes in a parked clinic van

exampleSpecs.audience: a sustainability entrepreneur selling through grocery partners
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether partners keep the kiosk after early shopper interest
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: a store manager explains the staff burden, forcing her to redesign the people proposition for partners
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Your customers love it," the grocery manager tells Petra, "but my cashiers hate the spill calls."

exampleSpecs.domain: family printer value promise and honest profit model
exampleSpecs.audience: a product lead tempted by a popular low-price device
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a low-friction offer can make money without hidden traps
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he challenges a value proposition that has no honest profit model beyond confusing refill costs
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Devon one prototype review to see the cheap printer was borrowing trouble from the ink drawer

exampleSpecs.domain: library after-hours pickup aligned with staffing
exampleSpecs.audience: a civic manager expanding access after hours
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether after-hours pickup works without unpaid staff strain
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the first plan gives patrons value but asks staff to absorb hidden work; lockers and shifts align it
exampleSpecs.firstImage: The library lobby is dark except for the holds shelf glowing behind locked glass
mustAvoid: generic library sorting example from chapter 7

exampleSpecs.domain: quiet dog-wash service tested against groomer strain and margin
exampleSpecs.audience: a small business owner testing a quieter grooming format
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a high-value experience works for owners, groomers, and margins
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she predicts buyer value is enough, then groomer strain and longer appointments force alignment
exampleSpecs.firstImage: What happens when every nervous dog needs twice the room and twice the time?

skillTargets: test alignment among value, profit, and people propositions
diagnose which proposition is weak in a promising offer
avoid calling buyer demand sustainable before the operating system works

tryThisNowSpec: Write three columns for one offer: buyer value, profit engine, people burden. Circle the column carrying the hidden strain.
